destination.title: He Buried His Daughter at Nine. 408,000 Have Filed. One Claim Paid $405.

candidate_payload_lines: Section 804 contains the sentence "Nothing in this subsection shall impair the right of any party to a trial by jury," and every claimant read it the obvious way.

On the sixth of February 2024 all four judges of the district signed a thirty-four-page order holding that the Act "does not unequivocally, affirmatively, and unambiguously provide plaintiffs the right to a jury trial," and struck the jury demand.
The court wrote that it expects both sides "to use their best efforts to achieve a global settlement by October 30, 2026." That is where this stands as this film goes out.
There was no suggestion, from anyone, that the water in the quarters had anything to do with anything, and there is no evidence that anyone at Camp Lejeune in 1985 connected the two.

There were families who had left in 1974 and scattered to Ohio and Texas and Florida and had no idea they had anything in common at all, because the one thing the Marine Corps had never done was tell them.
"Water highly contaminated with other chlorinated hydrocarbons — solvents!" That form has a number.
"'You have male breast cancer' were the words which greeted me and my wife on our 18th wedding anniversary." His name is Mike Partain.
"No further action was taken." What the agency found when it looked at itself first was not flattering.

And it took the statute of repose off the board entirely: "Any applicable statute of repose or statute of limitations… shall not apply to a claim under this section." Most remarkably, it lowered the burden of proof to a standard almost no plaintiff ever gets.
A claimant must show that the relationship between the water and the harm is "sufficient to conclude that a causal relationship is at least as likely as not." Fifty-fifty is enough.
The order contains a line that reads like an apology: "Congress could have made this dispute easy to resolve." The second reversal is the evidence.
In September 1985, a Marine Corps drill instructor named Jerry Ensminger lost his nine-year-old daughter to leukemia.
She was ill for nearly two and a half years, and the family was told what families are always told — that these things happen, and nobody is at fault.
He and his wife lived in base family housing at a place called Tarawa Terrace from 1973 to 1975.
Then he was sent to drill instructor school at Parris Island, and on the twentieth of December 1975 they left.
Nobody in the history of that base ever looked at a glass of water and thought about it for a second.
Half of American industry in 1965 kept solvent in open drums behind the shop.
But nobody at the base was measuring for any of that, because in the 1950s and 1960s and most of the 1970s nobody in the United States was.
era_note: Two eras, and they must not be mixed. The base story runs 1953-1987 on the North Carolina coastal plain: brick family quarters, washing lines, wells and pump houses, printed and hand-annotated laboratory forms, rotary telephones, typewriters. The legal story is present day, 2022-2026: a federal courthouse, filings, settlement meetings, modern offices. Modern stock footage is correct only for the second; anything modern inside the base years reads wrong.

shorts.angle: The Marine Corps' own laboratory wrote nine words about the drinking water in March 1981, and the form sat in a government file for sixteen years.
shorts.avoids: This Short is only the document and the six years of taps that stayed open. It never tells the father's story or the claims arithmetic the other two Shorts carry.
shorts.funnel_question_left_for_longform: Who was still drinking that water in the six years between the form and the last plant closing?
shorts.loop_join: L8 leaves the form still sitting in a records facility with the technician's sentence on it; L1 goes back to the day he wrote it down.

lines.text: In March 1981 the Army's own laboratory wrote nine words on a sample form from Camp Lejeune, ending with an exclamation mark.
source_lines: And then, on samples dated the ninth of March 1981, at Hadnot Point, the Army's own laboratory wrote the sentence that this entire case has turned on for four decades.
It is nine words long. It ends with an exclamation mark, which is not a thing analytical chemists put in remarks boxes.

lines.text: Water highly contaminated with other chlorinated hydrocarbons — solvents. That form has a number. It sat in a government file for sixteen years.
source_lines: "Water highly contaminated with other chlorinated hydrocarbons — solvents!" That form has a number.
It is CLW 0443, and it sat in a government file for sixteen years until a retired drill instructor asked for it.

lines.text: The technicians were not looking for solvents. They were testing for chlorination by-products, and the water was too contaminated to finish that test.
source_lines: They were not looking for solvents. They were looking for trihalomethanes, which are the by-products you get when you chlorinate water, and which every municipal system in America has to check.
Levels of these contaminants were so high so as to preclude THM testing.

lines.text: Nothing happened. That is the finding, and it needs no adjective. The wells kept running. The families kept drinking.
source_lines: Nothing happened. That is the finding, and it needs no adjective. The wells kept running. The families kept drinking.

lines.text: In 1982 a private laboratory said it again, in a letter to the Commanding General: more important from a health standpoint.
source_lines: In August his colleague Bruce Babson put it in a letter to the Commanding General
More important from a health standpoint. That is 1982.

lines.text: The contaminated wells at Hadnot Point came out of service between November 1984 and February 1985. The Tarawa Terrace plant closed in 1987.
source_lines: The contaminated wells at Hadnot Point came out of service between November 1984 and February 1985.
The Tarawa Terrace treatment plant, the one that had served the family housing, was not closed until 1987.

lines.text: It proves the institution measured its own water, wrote down that it was heavily contaminated, and never went to find the people drinking it.
source_lines: It proves that the institution measured its own water, wrote down that the water was heavily contaminated, and then took between three and six years to turn off the taps — and then did not go and find the people who had been drinking it.

lines.text: The form is still in a records facility: nine words and an exclamation mark, written by a technician who wrote down what he found.
source_lines: somewhere in a records facility the form from the ninth of March 1981 is still exactly what it always was — nine words and an exclamation mark
He wrote down what he found.

shorts.angle: A retired drill instructor with no legal or scientific training built the only archive of Camp Lejeune that exists, one Freedom of Information request at a time.
shorts.avoids: This Short is only the man and the binder. It does not read out the 1981 form, and it never reaches the claims, the court or the settlement figures.
shorts.funnel_question_left_for_longform: What was on the form he finally pried loose, and why had the families never been told?
shorts.loop_join: L8 says the binder is the only reason Camp Lejeune is known at all; L1 returns to the loss that sent him looking for it.

lines.text: In September 1985 a Marine Corps drill instructor lost his nine-year-old daughter to leukemia. Jerry Ensminger learned about the water twelve years later.
source_lines: In September 1985, a Marine Corps drill instructor named Jerry Ensminger lost his nine-year-old daughter to leukemia.
In August 1997 Jerry Ensminger learned that the water at Camp Lejeune had been contaminated.

lines.text: A federal health agency was proposing a study of children exposed in the womb at Camp Lejeune between 1968 and 1985.
source_lines: was proposing a study of childhood leukemia and non-Hodgkin's lymphoma among children exposed in the womb while their parents lived at Camp Lejeune between 1968 and 1985.

lines.text: His daughter had been conceived in that housing and had died of exactly that disease at exactly that age, more than a decade earlier.
source_lines: And the man whose daughter had been conceived in that housing, and had died of exactly that disease at exactly that age, found out about it by accident, more than a decade later, as a civilian.

lines.text: He was fifty-one, retired, with no legal training and no scientific training. He had twenty-four and a half years inside the institution instead.
source_lines: He was fifty-one years old, he was retired, he had no legal training and no scientific training, and what he had instead was twenty-four and a half years of learning how a military bureaucracy actually moves paper.

lines.text: He knew there would be paper. Somebody sampled that water. Somebody wrote a number on a form. Somebody filed it.
source_lines: He knew there would be paper. There is always paper. Somebody sampled that water. Somebody wrote a number on a form. Somebody signed the form and somebody filed it, and government files do not evaporate; they get boxed.

lines.text: Requests came back partial, late, or with the useful part removed. He put what came back in a ring binder, then a second binder.
source_lines: Requests that came back partial, requests that came back late, requests that came back with the useful part removed
He put what came back in a ring binder. Then he needed a second binder.

lines.text: Not a journalist, not a regulator, not a member of Congress. A retired drill instructor at a kitchen table in North Carolina.

lines.text: The binder grew for a quarter of a century. It is the reason anything is known about Camp Lejeune at all.

shorts.angle: Congress removed every legal barrier standing in front of Camp Lejeune claimants, and four years later one settled claim was paid four hundred and five dollars.
shorts.avoids: This Short is only the law and what it delivered. It does not tell the father's story, and it never quotes the 1981 laboratory form.
shorts.funnel_question_left_for_longform: What happens to four hundred and eight thousand claims when the court's October deadline passes?
shorts.loop_join: L8 ends on the claimants whose injuries had already killed them; L1 restates the two numbers that surround them — filed, and paid.

lines.text: Four hundred and eight thousand people filed Camp Lejeune claims. Roughly two thousand four hundred and forty-six have been paid.
source_lines: As of that filing, roughly two thousand four hundred and forty-six people had been paid. Out of four hundred and eight thousand who filed.

lines.text: Congress had removed every barrier. The Camp Lejeune Justice Act waived the government's immunity and took the statute of repose off the board entirely.
source_lines: Every wall was down.
It waived the government's immunity, including the discretionary-function defence that had beaten these claims before. And it took the statute of repose off the board entirely

lines.text: It lowered the burden of proof for causation to a standard almost no plaintiff ever gets. Fifty-fifty is enough.
source_lines: Most remarkably, it lowered the burden of proof to a standard almost no plaintiff ever gets.
Fifty-fifty is enough.

lines.text: All four judges of the district struck the jury demand, holding that the Act did not unambiguously provide a right to a jury trial.
source_lines: On the sixth of February 2024 all four judges of the district signed a thirty-four-page order holding that the Act "does not unequivocally, affirmatively, and unambiguously provide plaintiffs the right to a jury trial," and struck the jury demand.

lines.text: The court picked twenty-five bellwether plaintiffs across five diseases. Four years after the law passed, not one of those cases has been tried.
source_lines: To move things along, the court picked twenty-five bellwether plaintiffs
Not one of those cases has been tried. Four years after the law passed, there is no trial date.

lines.text: By June 2026 the government had settled just three of those twenty-five cases. Robert Fiolek, leukemia: ten thousand dollars.
source_lines: The United States had reached agreement on settlement amounts for three of the twenty-five bellwether cases.
Robert Fiolek, leukemia: ten thousand dollars.

lines.text: Edward Raymond, bladder cancer: twenty-four thousand dollars. Jose Vidana, non-Hodgkin's lymphoma: four hundred and five dollars. Paid, and the case dismissed.
source_lines: Edward Raymond, bladder cancer: twenty-four thousand dollars. Jose Vidana, non-Hodgkin's lymphoma: four hundred and five dollars.
Four hundred and five dollars. Paid, and the case dismissed.

lines.text: Of the offers the Navy approved, one thousand one hundred and fifty-one were for an injury that had already resulted in death.
source_lines: Of the offers the Navy approved, one thousand one hundred and fifty-one were claims for an injury that had already resulted in death
